title: Transit Commission Meeting
overview: The Wausau Transit Commission met on November 19, 2026, and unanimously approved four action items: issuing an RFP for new cash-only fare boxes, authorizing bids for replacement of exterior doors at the Metro Ride facility, authorizing bids for ceiling replacement at the facility, and aligning Metro Ride's procurement policy with the City of Wausau's. The commission also unanimously approved participation in a transit development planning study funded largely by a $120,000 state grant. Director Ron reported that 10 new Gillig buses have arrived and will be phased into service, while the Wisco mobile fare contract remains stalled over unresolved contract language concerns.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes of Preceding Meeting
discussions.body: The presiding officer noted a correction was needed because their own excused absence did not appear in the minutes. Alder Sarah Watson moved to approve the minutes as adjusted, and Christopher Williams seconded. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 4A: Permission to Issue RFP for New Fare Boxes
discussions.body: Transit Director Ron explained that the existing Genfair fare boxes installed in 1996 are failing and parts are unavailable. He proposed replacing them with simple, low-tech cash-only boxes with a lockable vault, funded by an 80/20 grant, noting that electronic fare boxes would cost roughly half a million dollars by comparison. Christopher Williams expressed strong support, and commission members asked about fare counting and anticipated use of electronic payment alternatives. Christopher Williams moved and Kathy Zorn seconded; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 4B: Permission to Replace Exterior Doors at Metro Ride Facility
discussions.body: Ron explained that the facility's original 1970s-era doors are rusted through and the building ranked at the bottom of a city-wide energy efficiency study. He emphasized the need to spend remaining 80/20 grant funds before they expire in March, and noted that selling the building in the future would benefit from improvements. Commission members questioned the wisdom of upgrading a building intended for replacement, but Ron estimated a new facility is likely a decade or more away. Christopher Williams moved and Kathy Zorn seconded; the motion to seek quotes passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 4C: Permission for Ceiling Replacement at Metro Ride Facility
discussions.body: Ron described the ceiling tiles as heavily water-stained and sagging from past roof leaks, noting the roof itself was replaced about five years ago. He said the work would be under $50,000 and would not require a full RFP — just three competitive bids — with results to come back at the next monthly meeting. Kathy Zorn moved and Christopher Williams seconded; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 4D: Permission to Update Metro Ride Procurement Policy to Match City of Wausau Policy
discussions.body: Ron sought commission approval to align Metro Ride's procurement dollar thresholds with those recently updated in the City of Wausau's policy, noting FTA regulations require Metro Ride to maintain its own separate policy. He said a finalized updated policy would return for a formal vote next month. Alder Watson asked clarifying questions about which version of the policy was current. A commission member moved to permit pursuing the ordinance alignment; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 4E: Permission for Transit Development Planning Study
discussions.body: Lori Mskimmons, Director of the Wausau MPO housed within Marathon County, explained that the MPO and Metro Ride are required by the FTA to update their transit development plan every five years. The study will examine unmet needs, service efficiency, and potential microtransit options, with the MPO committing $6,000, the state providing $120,000, and the city's match set at $24,000. Ron noted the FTA requirement and that Metro Ride has reserves and operational savings that should cover the $24,000 match. Alder Watson asked about budget sourcing; Ron expressed confidence in available reserves and grant offsets. Christopher Williams moved and Kathy Zorn seconded; the motion passed unanimously, with Ron noting it would also proceed to the Finance Committee and full Council.

discussions.item: 5A-C: Director's Reports — New Gillig Buses, CAD/AVL Update, Wisco Contract Update
discussions.body: Ron reported all 10 new Gillig buses funded by a VW grant have arrived on Metro Ride's property and will be phased into service starting after Thanksgiving, with the goal of having all running by end of December. He said the CAD/AVL real-time bus tracking system will go live to the public once the new buses are in service, though he cautioned that keeping detour information updated in real time has been a challenge. On the Wisco mobile fare system, Ron said the city attorney raised concerns about passenger fund protections if Milwaukee Transit were to drop UMO as the platform provider, and that Metro Ride is awaiting a response from Milwaukee Transit on revised contract language before moving forward.

title: Revised Administrative Policy Committee Meeting
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter's Administrative Policy Committee held its November 17, 2026 meeting, approving several budget-related recommendations including a $5,000 park grant match, a multi-item 2026 budget amendment, and health insurance renewals for two employee groups. Finance Director John Jacobs led extensive discussions on tax increment district closure timelines, the 2027 budget, and upcoming property revaluation — all of which carry significant long-term financial implications for village taxpayers. The committee also agreed by consensus to skip its December meeting and reconvene January 19, 2027.

discussions.body: The committee moved to approve all three sets of minutes together. During discussion, committee member Guy Fridl noted he had previously raised a question about whether areas along Maple Ridge Road have developable sewer and water capacity; the presiding officer directed that the question be noted in the minutes and referred to Public Works Director Greg for a response at a future meeting. The motion was approved 4-0.

discussions.item: Item F: Update on Estimated Closure Dates for All Tax Increment Districts
discussions.body: Finance Director John Jacobs provided a detailed overview of projected closure timelines for all four TIF districts. TID 3 was already closed in February 2026, eight years early, returning approximately $3 million in valuation to the tax roll and adding $1,139 to the levy in 2027 with a full effect of roughly $8,300 thereafter. TID 2 is projected to close by 2029 — five years early — which could add up to $219,000 to the tax levy by 2031; Jacobs noted the $863,200 borrowed in late 2024 must be spent or committed by October 2027 and may remain in TID 2 to fund Maple Ridge Road work. TID 4 is expected to close around 2031–2032 after going temporarily cash-flow negative. TID 1, boosted by a large distribution center project, could close by 2039 — five years early — adding approximately $140,000 annually to the levy by 2041. Jacobs declined to publicly state the distribution center's estimated market value, saying the developer had not yet disclosed it publicly, but confirmed $15 million as a first-year rough estimate. When asked about charging interest on the village's advance to TID 1, Jacobs said he would seek guidance from the village's financial advisor before making a recommendation.

discussions.item: Item G: 2027 Budget Presentation Highlights
discussions.body: Jacobs highlighted key elements of the adopted 2027 budget, noting the assessed tax rate rose 22 cents to $4.25 but that after the pending property revaluation — required by state law to be completed by end of 2027 — the rate will fall significantly, comparable to what occurred after the 2021 revaluation. He explicitly addressed social media claims that the rate would reach $5.00, calling them false and explaining that revaluation mechanics bring the assessed rate in line with the equalized rate. Budget additions include fully funding two new patrol officers (the second position still unfilled), a new utility operator starting January 1, a deputy clerk starting April 1, and a 3.5% cost-of-living wage increase across the board. Health insurance for non-police staff came in at 4% rather than the feared 8% increase.

discussions.item: Item H: December 2026 Assessed Tax Rates
discussions.body: Jacobs presented estimated combined tax rates for both Mosinee and D.C. Everest school district residents, noting the final numbers were expected before Thanksgiving. For Mosinee district taxpayers, the total rate is projected to rise roughly $1.04, or about 6%; the village's share of that increase (22 cents) is the third-lowest among taxing jurisdictions, with Marathon County's increase (42 cents, 8.4%) being the largest. D.C. Everest district residents face an estimated 85-cent total increase, or about 4.9%. Jacobs reminded residents that the village comprises about 23% of the total tax bill and cannot answer questions about other jurisdictions' charges.

discussions.item: Item I: 2026 Budget Amendment #5 — Park Grant Matching Funds
discussions.body: Jacobs presented a $5,000 transfer from the general fund to the park fund to match a grant from the Wausau and Marathon County Park and Recreation Foundation, consistent with a prior parks committee recommendation to the village board. The committee moved to recommend board approval. The motion carried 4-0 on a roll call vote.

discussions.item: Item J: 2026 Budget Amendment #6 — General Fund and TID 3 Fund
discussions.body: Jacobs outlined a series of revenue and expenditure adjustments to bring the 2026 general fund budget in line with actual activity. New revenues include a $54,370 oil pipeline termination state aid payment (previously unknown) and a $42,855 transfer from the closing TID 3 fund. Expenditure increases cover ambulance run overruns (projected at 492 runs vs. 420 budgeted), village attorney costs roughly doubling to ~$60,000 due to a personnel investigation and a surge in open records requests, $25,000 in additional municipal building repairs including a $14,500 hot water heater replacement, fuel surcharge fees for refuse and recycling totaling ~$57,000, and miscellaneous solid waste and cleanup week overruns. The contingency reserve draw was reduced from $60,000 to $38,815 to offset these changes. The TID 3 fund closure transfers were also included. Guy Fridl moved the recommendation; Mary Solheim seconded; approved 4-0 on roll call.

discussions.item: Item K: 2027–2029 Health Insurance — Team Care
discussions.body: Jacobs reported that Team Care unexpectedly provided a three-year proposal, locking in a 4% premium increase for 2027 ($469.50/month), a maximum 4% increase for 2028 ($488.30), and a maximum 6% increase for 2029 ($517.60). Approximately 15–20 non-police-union employees are covered. The committee expressed positive surprise at the multi-year offer. Misty Swanson moved to recommend board approval; Guy Fridl seconded; approved 4-0 on roll call. Jacobs noted the proposal must be signed by December 6.

discussions.item: Item L: 2027 Health Insurance — United Health Care (Police Union Group)
discussions.body: Jacobs presented a 14.2% premium increase from United Health Care for the seven-member police union group, raising the monthly premium from approximately $14,000 to $16,417. He noted staff is exploring whether this group could be moved to Team Care, but complications include two employees currently waiving coverage (Team Care only allows one waiver), individual rate variability by age and family size, and a submission deadline of December 12. Guy Fridl moved to recommend the quote to the board for consideration in light of additional future information; Mary Solheim seconded; approved 4-0 on roll call.

discussions.item: Future Agenda Items and December Meeting Cancellation
discussions.body: Committee member Guy Fridl suggested a future agenda discussion on building reserve funds modeled after Marathon County's approach, crediting Jacobs for stabilizing village finances but expressing a desire to go further. Jacobs and the presiding officer discussed the impracticality of a December 15 APC meeting given that the December 28 village board meeting was likely canceled, meaning any recommendations couldn't be acted on until January 11. By consensus the committee agreed to cancel the December 15 meeting and reconvene January 19, 2027, when financial audit materials or internal year-end statements may be available.

title: Plan Commission Meeting
overview: The Wausau Plan Commission held its November 17, 2026 meeting, addressing a contested rezoning request for 317 East Kent Street and reviewing the housing chapter of the city's updated comprehensive plan. The rezoning request from urban mixed-use to heavy industrial failed on a 2-2 tie vote and will advance to the full City Council for a decision at its December 8 meeting. The comprehensive plan housing chapter discussion covered affordability, housing supply, and new state legislation that will require significant attention in future meetings.

discussions.item: Approval of October 20, 2026 Regular Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: A motion to approve the minutes was made by a member identified as True Blood and seconded by a member identified as Bugamman. No corrections were offered and the minutes were approved unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Public Hearing: Rezoning of 317 East Kent Street from Urban Mixed-Use to Heavy Industrial
discussions.body: Three members of the public spoke during the hearing. A resident from Mount View Boulevard opposed the rezoning, citing proximity to the Eau Claire River Conservancy — approximately 200 feet away — and risk of stormwater runoff contaminating the conservancy's 49.3 acres of pine, hardwoods, and wetlands. A second resident from Sturgeon Road expressed conditional support, noting the nearby Holtze-Krauss landfill history and arguing that if the operator — which he believed to be a local contracting company — complies with city and DNR rules, it would be unlikely to harm the conservancy. A representative of the Friends of the Lower Eau Claire River Advocacy Group opposed the rezoning, arguing that stormwater from the 5.4-acre site drains directly through an HDPE culvert to the river wetlands with no filtration, and that heavy industrial zoning runs with the land and could allow more onerous future uses even if the current operator is responsible.

discussions.item: Discussion and Possible Action: Rezoning of 317 East Kent Street from Urban Mixed-Use to Heavy Industrial
discussions.body: City staff explained the applicant sought the zoning change to construct a salt shed storage building and attached office, and that a 2016 conditional use permit for soil sifting and compost storage was voided in the comprehensive zoning rewrite, leaving the site as a legal non-conforming use that cannot be expanded without rezoning. Staff recommended denial, stating the proposal does not advance the purposes of the zoning title, is inconsistent with the comprehensive plan's future land use designation of suburban residential, and constitutes spot zoning. A member identified as Bugamman moved to approve the rezoning in the affirmative; the motion was seconded by a member identified as True Blood. The vote failed 2-2 and will be forwarded to the City Council for its December 8 meeting.

discussions.item: Wausau Comprehensive Plan Update – Chapter 3 Housing
discussions.body: Sam Wessel of the North Central Wisconsin Regional Planning Commission walked the commission through the draft housing chapter, covering housing cost trends, supply and demand dynamics, cost burden rates, unhoused population data, housing type variety, and state legislative changes. Commissioners asked pointed questions about what is driving higher rental prices relative to local incomes, potential ordinance barriers to housing development, incentivizing multigenerational housing, discouraging land hoarding, mobile home and manufactured housing options, condominium financing barriers, and corporate ownership of rental properties. Staff noted Wausau's recently rewritten zoning code — which won a statewide planning award for addressing missing middle housing — puts the city ahead of most Wisconsin communities on the zoning side. Discussion of Act 173, which requires densities to be written into future land use map categories and provides automatic approval for projects meeting those densities, was flagged as requiring several future meetings to address properly.

A second resident offered conditional support, referencing the history of the nearby Holtze-Krauss landfill and stating that if the applicant obeys city and DNR rules and operates the property as well as the company maintains other properties in the city, there would likely be no harm to the conservancy. A representative of the Friends of the Lower Eau Claire River Advocacy Group opposed the rezoning, citing a stormwater drainage path from the site directly to the river wetlands with no filtration, and expressed concern that heavy industrial zoning running with the land could permit more harmful uses by future owners.

title: Board Special Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board held a special meeting focused on the Hub City Wind Project's proposed Joint Development Agreement (JDA) from Alliant Energy and a separate issue involving Bug Tussle's failure to make required bond payments. Seven members of the public spoke overwhelmingly against the JDA, and board supervisors expressed strong disappointment with Alliant's response to the county's earlier resolution, with the board ultimately voting to go into closed session to discuss strategy on both matters.

discussions.item: Public comment time limit appeal
discussions.body: Board Chair Gibbs initially ruled that seven public speakers would divide 15 minutes (approximately two minutes each). Supervisor Dickinson moved to appeal the ruling and allow three minutes per speaker, seconded by another supervisor. Supervisors Gal, Straw, Sundowski, and Dickinson all spoke in favor of three minutes, arguing the meeting was specifically called for this issue and constituents deserved a full hearing. The appeal passed and three minutes per speaker was granted.

discussions.item: Public comment — Hub City Wind Project and JDA
discussions.body: Seven speakers addressed the board, all opposing the proposed JDA with Alliant Energy. Speakers raised concerns about aviation safety near the proposed turbines, inadequate health and safety protections in the JDA, wildlife migration impacts, road damage liability, shadow flickering, Alliant's honesty based on its track record at other projects, vague contract language, and lack of community benefit provisions. Debbie Stone, president and CEO of Wisconsin for Local Control, offered professional regulatory and legal assistance to the county, noting her organization is an intervenor in Alliant's Columbia Wind PSC case. Tren Spindler, chair of the towns' intergovernmental committee, urged the county not to sign the JDA and instead update its comprehensive plan, zoning, and ordinances, warning that weak county zoning was why the project was sited in Marathon County.

discussions.item: Overview of Alliant Energy response to Resolution 55-26 and potential next steps
discussions.body: County Administrator summarized that in October the board passed Resolution 55-26 requesting a contractual agreement from Alliant addressing the advisory committee's concerns; Alliant's draft response was included in the board packet and shared with impacted township representatives. He outlined options including engaging in negotiations, refusing to negotiate, and preparing for PSC intervention. Supervisor Robinson, chair of the local impact advisory committee, said he was 'terribly disappointed' in Alliant's response, calling it a 'canned JDA' that ignored community input and did not go beyond statutory requirements, and said he was torn between negotiating and preparing for intervention. Supervisor Dickinson argued the county has no leverage with Alliant and called on the board to take a firm stand. Supervisor Sundowski called the JDA 'garbage' and cited a constituent survey of 1,395 respondents showing a vast majority opposed, with only three of 150 forum attendees in favor. Supervisors Cavelli, Ritter, and Morash raised concerns about whether the county's current legal counsel (Atol's law firm) has a conflict of interest given that Alliant Energy is listed as a corporate partner of the Wisconsin Counties Association. Multiple supervisors called for hiring outside legal counsel or working with Wisconsin for Local Control.

discussions.item: Bug Tussle bonding and loan agreement update
discussions.body: The county administrator reported that Bug Tussle failed to make a sufficient deposit into its debt service fund to cover required bond payments. Marathon County's share of the 2021 $25 million conduit bond issuance is $347,491, due by April 8 of next year. The county also has a separate direct $8 million loan with Bug Tussle entered in 2024. Supervisor Dickinson publicly apologized for his role in supporting the Bug Tussle contract despite community warnings, saying he was 'embarrassed.' The administrator recommended closed session to discuss legal and negotiation strategy related to the non-payment notices.

discussions.item: Motion to go into closed session
discussions.body: Supervisor Cyver moved that the Alliant Energy discussion remain in open session to keep the public informed, but county counsel advised the cleaner procedural path was to go into closed session only for Bug Tussle while leaving Alliant in open session. Board Chair Gibbs argued he wanted to preserve negotiating strategy on the Alliant matter as well, stating he was not in favor of the JDA but wanted closed-session discussion on intervention strategy. Supervisor Luer ultimately moved to go into closed session covering both Bug Tussle bond non-payment strategy and Alliant Energy JDA next steps; Supervisor Peak seconded. The motion passed on a roll call vote and the board recessed into closed session.

publicComment: Seven speakers addressed the board. The first speaker, a resident of the Town of McMillan, raised concerns about helicopter flight routes to Marshfield Children's Hospital being endangered by 685-foot turbines and the lack of health and safety provisions in the JDA. The second speaker questioned whether board members had read Alliant's contract, criticized its vague language, and accused Alliant of not addressing concerns raised by the advisory committee. The third speaker, Christine Se Haver of the Town of McMillan, spoke on behalf of residents of the six affected townships (McMillan, Day, Green Valley, Cleveland, Oplane, and Brighton), urging the county not to ignore community research or conduct future discussions in closed session, and warning that the Stonemark Wind project was next. The fourth speaker, Jerry Fischer of the Town of Day, described his private airstrip and raised aviation safety concerns about turbine vortices, and questioned whether the county's $250,000 set-aside for road damage was sufficient. The fifth speaker, Joe Bergen, urged the board to discard Alliant's 14-page JDA document in favor of Farmland First's analysis, and urged serious engagement with the affected townships. The sixth speaker, Debbie Stone, president and CEO of Wisconsin for Local Control, described her organization's role as intervenor in the Columbia Wind PSC case and offered professional regulatory, legal, and engineering support to Marathon County. The seventh speaker, Tren Spindler, chair of the towns' intergovernmental committee, urged the county to reject the JDA and instead update its comprehensive plan, zoning, and ordinances in partnership with the townships, warning that if the county failed to act, townships might consider leaving county zoning to establish their own protections.

title: Board of Trustees
overview: The Village of Weston Board of Trustees held its regular meeting on Monday, November 16, 2026, highlighted by a contentious 4-3 vote to adopt the 2027 operating budget and an equally divided 4-3 vote on the debt service and capital funds budgets, with the three newer trustees (Beck, Clark, and Olson) voting against both over concerns about excessive borrowing and spending of TIF district closure funds. The board also approved a $4 million loan for the Mountain Bay Metro Police Department headquarters, approved a Mack Mueller Park master plan (without the cost estimate), and authorized an aquatic center building and pool evaluation funded from unassigned general fund balance rather than borrowing.

discussions.item: Public Hearing: 2027 Budget
discussions.body: Finance staff presented the balanced 2027 budget totaling $10,794,907 in revenues and expenditures, with a total levy of $9,925,976 — an increase of $1,389,554 — driven partly by the closure of TIF District No. 1. Staff noted the village tax rate would decrease slightly to 5.54, though Marathon County's budget would add approximately 25 cents to the overall tax bill. Two members of the public spoke in opposition during the public hearing, with one arguing the board squandered a generational opportunity from TIF closure funds by maximizing borrowing rather than paying down debt, and another raising concerns about taking on new multi-million dollar projects while existing ones remain unfinished.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-028 – Adopt 2027 Operating Budget
discussions.body: The motion to adopt the 2027 operating budget was moved by Trustee Ermeling and seconded by Trustee Zeyghami. Trustees Beck, Clark, and Olson all stated they remained opposed to the budget due to excessive borrowing and missed opportunities to use TIF funds for debt reduction or savings rather than recurring costs. Trustees supporting the budget argued that the debt service reflects projects the full board had previously voted to pursue and that new firefighter funding was a key community priority. The resolution passed 4-3, with Beck, Clark, and Olson voting nay.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-029 – Adopt Debt Service, Special Revenue, Capital Projects, and Proprietary Funds 2027 Budgets
discussions.body: Moved by Trustee Lopes-Serrao and seconded by Trustee Zeyghami, this companion budget resolution covering non-general funds also passed 4-3. Trustees Beck, Clark, and Olson again voted nay, citing the same concerns about over-borrowing and lack of prioritization among capital projects. No additional extended debate occurred on this resolution beyond what had already been discussed on the operating budget.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-027 – Authorize $4 Million Borrowing for Mountain Bay Metro Police Department Headquarters
discussions.body: The regional president of One Community Bank attended to answer questions about the promissory note. Key discussion centered on the prepayment language in the loan documents, which the bank clarified allows additional principal payments with no penalty but does not eliminate the obligation to continue monthly payments. Trustee Zeyghami moved approval; Village President Maloney seconded. The resolution passed 6-1, with one trustee voting nay.

discussions.item: Mack Mueller Park Master Plan and Cost Estimate
discussions.body: Sean from Parks presented the updated master plan for Mack Mueller Park, which includes pickle ball courts, a basketball court, a tennis court, a band shell, and other amenities, with a broad cost estimate of approximately $4 million. Trustee Lopes-Serrao moved to approve only the master plan — not the cost estimate — explaining that approving a cost estimate was unnecessary since no spending is authorized and a more precise figure would be needed for grants. Trustee Olson seconded. Several trustees noted the master plan is required to be eligible for state and federal grant funding and that no dollars are currently allocated. The motion passed 6-1, with one trustee voting nay.

discussions.item: Aquatic Center Evaluation
discussions.body: Sean presented two proposals for an updated aquatic center evaluation — one from Raymaker and Associates for $16,000 (covering both pool and building, with $14,000 for pool and $2,000 for building) and one from WaterTech for $16,800 (pool only). Trustee Beck moved to approve the Raymaker proposal for both the building and pool evaluation. After Trustee Olson raised objections to funding the evaluation through capital borrowing, the motion was amended to specify funding from the unassigned general fund balance rather than borrowing. Trustee Clark seconded the amended motion, which passed. Staff noted the unassigned general fund balance is currently approximately $440,000 above the village's 33% policy threshold.

discussions.item: Business 51 Storm Pond Construction Intergovernmental Agreement
discussions.body: Public Works Director Michael presented the intergovernmental agreement with Rothschild and Schofield for constructing a storm water retention pond within the Highway 29/Business 51 cloverleaf right-of-way. Discussion focused on the village's share growing from an estimated 125 pounds of phosphorus credit to 225 pounds, increasing the village's cost share to approximately 90% of the roughly $2.8 million construction cost. The board amended the agreement to cap the village's exposure at 5% above the bid cost estimate before requiring further board approval, then approved the amended agreement unanimously.

discussions.item: Ross Avenue Riverbend to Paul's Intergovernmental Agreement
discussions.body: Trustee Lopes-Serrao moved approval and Trustee Zeyghami seconded. A resident speaker during public comment had raised concerns that the agreement language was vague and amounted to subsidizing the Town of Weston. Trustee Zeyghami noted that while the town benefits from storm water improvements, any annexation of land along the corridor would ultimately benefit the village's tax base. The agreement was approved without amendment; the board did not add specific dollar amounts or percentages to the agreement language despite the public comment request.

discussions.item: Police Department Update and Communications
discussions.body: The police chief reported 2,223 calls for the month, 471 traffic stops, and 307 citations. He provided an update on the new police headquarters construction, noting footings are in, frost walls are being poured, walls are scheduled for delivery December 18, and the sewer lateral was connected the day of the meeting; a mid-to-late next year completion estimate was offered. Trustee Clark raised concerns that video updates on the police department's website had not been posted since August 27 and that the public had no easily accessible source for information about the TC Energy pipeline easement issue. The chief committed to improving communications. The chief also announced the department would no longer assist with residential lockouts, citing negative community feedback and liability concerns.

discussions.item: Closed Session – Return to Open Session
discussions.body: The board returned from closed session at 9:29 p.m. A motion passed to move forward with a right-of-way purchase offer (the agreed-upon amount for a strip of land related to the Ross Avenue/Metro to Alderson project). The administrator's annual evaluation was deferred to the December meeting by unanimous vote to allow more time.

publicComment: Two speakers addressed the board during the public hearing on the 2027 budget. The first speaker spoke at length in opposition, arguing the board wasted a generational opportunity from the TIF district closure by spending every available dollar rather than paying down debt, praised the three trustees who voted against the capital borrowing plan, and criticized the four trustees who supported the budget for leaving a long-term debt burden. The second speaker asked the board to complete existing projects before taking on new ones such as a new police headquarters and a new park development, raised privacy concerns about flock cameras that other communities have removed, and urged the board to prioritize current residents over development-driven spending. During general public comment, three additional residents spoke. One questioned the lack of an organizational chart for committee appointments on the agenda, raised concerns about the intergovernmental agreement language for the Ross Avenue project, and urged the board to have the village attorney review it. A second speaker criticized the pickle ball court plans for Mack Mueller Park, questioned the reported $2 million concession stand figure, and argued large capital projects like the police headquarters should have gone to a referendum. A third speaker, who also spoke during the public hearing, expressed broader frustration with the budget and village spending, referenced concerns about flock cameras, criticized incomplete park projects, and drew the board's attention to a letter from a named community member distributed at the meeting regarding Mack Mueller Park.

committee: Finance and HR Committee, Village of Weston
overview: The Village of Weston Finance and HR Committee met on November 16 and took action on accounts receivable write-offs and 2026 budget amendments, both of which were approved unanimously for forwarding to the village board. The committee deadlocked 3-3 on a motion to recommend Option G for sanitary sewer rate increases, with the item deferred to the December 21 meeting for updated financial figures.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: One resident, identified as Jim, spoke about the budget amendments on page 86, questioning $20,000 and $6,000 line items for computer equipment and asking what specific equipment was being purchased and whether purchases had already been made. He also questioned the $20,000 allocated to fix the boardroom audio system, noting the audio has not worked properly since the data system was installed over five years ago and arguing it was improper to budget funds for a project without a contract or firm price tag.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes
discussions.body: Minutes from the previous meeting were approved without discussion. A motion was made and seconded; the vote was unanimous in favor.

discussions.item: Work Product Transmittals: October Budget Status Reports, TIF 1 and TIF 2, Legal Details
discussions.body: Committee members reviewed the reports with limited questions. One member asked whether refuse and recycling invoices were paid to date and was told there is a one-month billing delay. Another member asked about a $240 charge for a pet open records request on top of a prior $1,560 charge, and staff confirmed it was a timing error and should be the final billing. A question was raised about when salaries would move from TIF funds back to the general fund; staff said the TIF closure audit is still in progress with no definitive date. The transmittals were acknowledged and approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Accounts Receivable Write-Off Transfers to Tax Roll
discussions.body: Staff presented a list of unpaid accounts receivable to be written off and placed on the property tax roll for collection. Committee members raised questions about the village's billing policy, noting that an older 2018 policy called for three reminder statements and 1.5% monthly interest accrual, while the current 2020 policy calls for only one additional statement. Staff acknowledged the interest accrual provision has not been followed and recommended updating the policy to reflect actual practice. One committee member noted that a recently listed debtor had personally called the individual, who paid that morning after being informed of the bill. The committee approved the write-offs as presented and directed staff to bring the accounts receivable policy back for review at a future meeting.

discussions.item: 2026 Budget Amendments
discussions.body: Staff presented budget amendments, explaining that many line items in the 40-series funds reflect projects already approved through debt borrowing and are being formally coded into accounts. Questions were raised about carryover items from 2025 including server equipment, Kennedy Park work, and road projects not completed before winter. A committee member asked about the $20,000 boardroom audio improvement; staff acknowledged estimates coming in are higher than $20,000 and that the figure was a placeholder to signal commitment to the project. Staff also explained that pickle ball court funds were reallocated after a planned partnership with a pickle ball organization fell through, and that a Mach Miller master plan including pickle ball courts would be presented to the board that same evening. The amendments were approved unanimously with a recommendation to the village board.

discussions.item: Sanitary Sewer Rates
discussions.body: Staff and committee engaged in extended discussion of eight rate increase options (A through H) for 2027 sewer rates, driven by rising costs from the Rib Mountain Metropolitan Sewage District, which accounts for roughly 50% of the sewer budget and is mid-construction on a capital project financed by a 20-year clean water fund loan. The Public Works and Utility Committee had recommended Option F, which would generate an estimated net income of $318,000 in 2027. Several committee members expressed preference for Option G as a middle ground, while others questioned whether the financial projections were reliable given discrepancies between staff narrative and the income statement figures. A motion was made to recommend Option G; the motion failed on a 3-3 tie vote. The committee reached consensus to defer the item to the December 21 meeting so staff could return with reconciled and updated financial figures.

publicComment: One speaker, identified as Jim, addressed the committee. He questioned two line items in the budget amendments — $20,000 and $6,000 for computer equipment (asking what specific equipment and whether purchases had been made) and $20,000 for boardroom audio improvements — arguing it was improper to budget funds for a project with no contract or firm price tag. He noted the boardroom audio system has been faulty for over five years.

title: Plan Commission Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Plan Commission held its November 16, 2026 meeting, approving recommendations on a septic tank ordinance amendment, the Green Tree Trails subdivision final plat, and a stormwater maintenance agreement for the County Road XX distribution center. The commission also received updates on the Pleasant Haven subdivision proposal for the former FAA site, discussed upcoming zoning code review priorities, and flagged traffic safety concerns on Pleasant Road near growing residential development.

discussions.item: Motion to Reorder Agenda
discussions.body: The chair moved to shift Item 8G (zoning code review) to after new business items to accommodate the energy levels and public present for those discussions. The motion was seconded and passed 7-0 with no discussion.

discussions.item: Public Hearing: Chapter 508 Septic Tank Ordinance Amendment
discussions.body: No members of the public appeared to speak at the public hearing. The chair announced no sign-ups and closed the hearing without testimony.

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes - July 20 and July 27, 2026
discussions.body: Bruce moved and Dick seconded approval of both sets of meeting minutes. One commissioner noted the minutes lacked a 'prepared by' attribution, which staff acknowledged as an oversight related to catching up after a clerk departure. Minutes were approved 7-0.

discussions.item: Community Development Director Report
discussions.body: Community Development Director Nathan reported on several developments: the DNR notified the village of a Rothschild dam failure analysis requiring updated floodplain maps within roughly a year; the Pleasant Haven subdivision application has been submitted for the former FAA site, requiring both a rezoning and a public hearing likely at the December 21st meeting; and he flagged two zoning code gaps — the lack of a use variance provision and the potential need for zoning changes to enable residential Tax Increment Districts, a new statewide tool. He urged commissioners to confirm December 21st availability soon so a public hearing notice can be published by December 1st.

discussions.item: Chapter 508-37 Septic Tank Ordinance Amendment
discussions.body: Rick Grundman recused himself. The ordinance amendment would allow restricted use of septic tanks within the village sewer service area under specific criteria including a 400-foot distance threshold, minimum 5-acre parcel, and no more than seven months of use per year. A commissioner asked about the basis for those numbers; a commissioner who sits on the utility committee explained they came from DPW Director Greg Almond and the utility foreman, informed by a specific case involving the school's concessions operation. Bruce moved and Dick seconded approval; the motion carried 6-0 (with Grundman recused) and will go to the village board.

discussions.item: Green Tree Trails Subdivision Final Plat and Draft Development Agreement
discussions.body: Nathan reported the final plat conforms with the previously approved preliminary plat from September, with one addition of access detail for the stormwater pond. Developer representative Bill Schofield (Pilgrims Landing, Menomonee Falls) addressed the commission, disclosing several key items: an emergency gated access to Nick Avenue is under contract with PGA Construction, funded by developer J. Shutey; the development is phased over potentially five to seven years with Phase 1 (lots on Pleasant/Pine), Phase 2 (interior lots and road), and Phase 3 (northern section); and Lot 54 is proposed to be sold ahead of its phase due to its proximity to a neighbor's patio, as a goodwill resolution. Commissioners asked about emergency access adequacy; one commissioner with nearly 20 years of emergency services experience said dead-end subdivisions are routinely handled and was not concerned. A commissioner raised traffic safety on Pleasant Road, noting a rear-end accident that evening. Jessica moved and Rick seconded to recommend board approval of the final plat; the motion passed 7-0 on a roll call vote.

discussions.item: Stormwater Maintenance Agreement - 2027 WASA LLC Distribution Center, 1619 County Road XX
discussions.body: Nathan explained the stormwater maintenance agreement fulfills a condition of the site plan approval granted last spring for the large distribution facility on County Road XX. A 170-page stormwater management report was received in September. The agreement ensures ongoing maintenance of the stormwater infiltration system by any future property owner. Bruce moved and Rick seconded to recommend board authorization; the motion passed 7-0.

discussions.item: Zoning Code Review (Item 8G)
discussions.body: Commissioners discussed priorities for zoning code updates. Nathan flagged the lack of a use variance provision (illustrated by a Wilson High School parcel situation involving TID restrictions), driveway clarity, and the need to enable residential TID districts which may require smaller lot size allowances. Commissioners also discussed the potential for mixed-use zoning provisions, noting the existing mixed-use TID district has developed mostly residential. Nathan agreed to compile his running list of code issues for the next meeting agenda. The discussion was informational with no action taken.

discussions.item: Future Agenda Items
discussions.body: A commissioner raised traffic and pedestrian safety concerns on Pleasant Road/Camp Phillips Road, citing a rear-end accident that evening and the lack of a pedestrian pathway, noting that Green Tree Trails and Pleasant Haven will add significant new residents to the area. The group suggested raising this at the board level, researching any existing county traffic studies, and engaging county board members. The appeals process for conditional use permits was also mentioned as a code review item. No formal action was taken.

publicComment: Bill Schofield of Pilgrims Landing, Menomonee Falls, signed up for public comment but chose to address the commission during the Green Tree Trails agenda item instead. No other members of the public offered comment. No speakers appeared at the Chapter 508 public hearing.

title: City Council Public Health & Safety Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Public Health & Safety Committee met in November 2026, addressing liquor and tobacco license applications including a provisional approval for a former fuel station under new ownership, a formal expression of concern regarding M&R Bar (Richard Gordon), and updates on the fire department apprenticeship program and a homelessness strategic plan. The committee approved a provisional liquor and tobacco license for the new fuel station operator and unanimously approved an emergency management services agreement with Marathon County.

discussions.item: Various License Applications (excluding Fuel On)
discussions.body: The committee moved to approve all license applications as presented with the exception of the Fuel On location, which was taken up separately. Alder True Blood moved, Alder Watson seconded, and the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Fuel On (Sunny Express) Provisional Liquor License and Tobacco License
discussions.body: City Clerk Cody presented a timeline showing the business was sold on September 23, 2026, and operated without a license for approximately 29 days before the city was notified on October 5. The new owner applied for a license on October 21 and had been in compliance since October 5. Captain Melinda Pauls confirmed the business had been compliant with checks for both alcohol and tobacco over the prior two months. Discussion arose over whether to grant the tobacco license alongside the provisional liquor license or wait until the 60-day provisional period ended; Alder Solonsky raised concerns about whether tobacco could be revisited if the provisional liquor license was not converted. Alder Watson moved to approve both the provisional liquor license per the liquor review committee's recommendation and the cigarette/tobacco license; Alder Lukans seconded. The motion passed unanimously. Alder True Blood noted that background information on the compliance gap should have been included in the committee packet.

discussions.item: Formal Expression of Concern: M&R Station, Richard Gordon DBA M&R Station LLC
discussions.body: Richard Gordon appeared to respond to a 100-point demerit assessment for failure to maintain an orderly premises related to a shooting incident. Gordon disputed characterizations of the event, arguing it was a premeditated attack by outsiders targeting a specific victim and that his staff had no way to know a shooting had occurred. Captain Pauls and Deputy Chief Payton testified that the suspect's vehicle had been parked in M&R's lot waiting, that both suspect and victim had been inside M&R together, and that a named suspect stated a staff member announced a 'BB gun' had been fired — indicating staff may have been aware of the incident without notifying police. Alder Lukans noted the demerit system functions as a strict liability standard for maintaining orderly premises. The committee was also informed by property manager Stacy Holt and attorney Karina Fischer that the property owners have issued a 28-day notice to Gordon and will proceed with eviction if he has not vacated by November 30. City staff clarified there is no formal process for removing assessed demerit points and that at 100 points no automatic action is triggered; revocation at a future hearing would be required to prevent Gordon from holding a license for 12 months. No formal vote or action was taken on this item.

discussions.item: Emergency Management Service Agreement with Marathon County
discussions.body: Alder True Blood moved to approve the emergency management service agreement with Marathon County as submitted; Alder Solonsky seconded. The motion passed unanimously with no debate.

discussions.item: Wausau Fire Department Quarter 3 2026 Report
discussions.body: The fire chief highlighted that the apprenticeship program formally launched September 28, with nine apprentices beginning an 18-month program covering EMT basic, Firefighter 1, Firefighter 2, and paramedic credentials. The department currently has six vacancies; three qualified firefighter-paramedics will start in December, reducing the gap to three. The apprenticeship program is intended to address future vacancies on an ongoing basis.

discussions.item: Homelessness Framework and Strategic Plan Update
discussions.body: Marathon County Public Health Coordinator Tracy Duranti's colleague presented an update on the foundational framework, noting a steering committee has been formed with city and county representation including Tracy Duranti from the police department and Randy Fifick from community development. Since August, over 120 unduplicated intake surveys of people experiencing homelessness have been collected through partner agencies. A daylong strategic planning session with over 30 community partners was held to inform the plan. The strategic plan draft will be presented to the committee in December for feedback, with a formal launch and joint city-county vote scheduled for January 26 at the civic engagement center.

publicComment: Three speakers offered public comment. Stacy Holt, property manager for BRH LLC (owner of the M&R Bar premises at 818 South 3rd Avenue), informed the committee that tenant Richard Gordon has been given a 28-day notice to vacate by November 30 and that the owners intend to proceed with eviction if he does not comply. Attorney Karina Fischer of [inaudible] Fischer confirmed the same and offered a copy of the notice to the clerk. Rodney Larson of Stockbridge, Wisconsin, attempted to raise concerns about Sunny Express operating tobacco sales without a license at multiple locations including Stevens Point; the chair ruled most of his testimony out of order as it concerned locations outside the city's jurisdiction, though Larson argued the same district manager oversees the Rib Mountain location under review.

overview: The Wausau City Council Infrastructure and Facilities Committee met and approved several items related to the South 11th Avenue reconstruction project affecting Kolbe and Kolbe Millwork, including handicap parking additions and multiple driveway variances. discussions.body: Staff explained the request came from Church of the Resurrection to add two more handicap stalls, and that two stalls added during the Second Street reconstruction had not been codified in the ordinance. The committee moved to approve the item to both add new stalls and clean up the ordinance. The motion passed unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Preliminary Resolution for Special Assessment for 2027 Street Construction Projects
discussions.body: Staff described the item as self-explanatory, noting approval would allow the city to set public hearings on special assessments, typically in December, in order to begin bidding projects. The motion was seconded by Wisowsky and passed unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Kolbe and Kolbe Millwork Driveway and Approach Variances (Items 4C–4F)
discussions.body: Staff explained that the South 11th Avenue reconstruction project required coordinating with Kolbe and Kolbe Millwork, whose campus straddles the road, over multiple meetings. The committee approved lay-down curb instead of full-head curb to preserve perpendicular parking at 1323 South 11th Avenue, waived the concrete approach requirement (staff noted asphalt costs roughly one-quarter the price of concrete at approximately $2 versus $8.50 per square foot), and approved two additional oversized driveways at 1330 and 1320 South 11th Avenue. A question about stormwater impact of the larger driveway was answered by staff, who called it minimal. All four items passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Recommendation to Extend Sidewalk on South 11th Avenue from Chellis Street to Fleith Street
discussions.body: Staff proposed adding sidewalk on the west side of 11th Avenue primarily to provide safe passage for Kolbe workers crossing to the manufacturing facility, with future connectivity potential toward 3M Park. Questions were raised about cost (staff said it would be a 50/50 cost share but did not have figures available) and whether bike lanes were planned (confirmed they were not). The motion was initially overlooked before being made and seconded by Alderman Martin; the item passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Boulevard Beautification Special Committee Formation
discussions.body: Kilian announced the formation of a special committee (not a subcommittee, as it includes public members) authorized by the October 27 council resolution. Appointed members include Alder Wiskowski as chair, city engineer Alan Wislowski PE, and citizen members Tim Hau, Dave Nutting, and Trevor Frank. All appointments are pending city council approval at the next meeting. Discussion briefly touched on a possible pre-Christmas organizational meeting, though some members noted travel conflicts in December.

discussions.item: City-Owned Vacant Parcels
discussions.body: Alder Wiskowski raised the topic, expressing interest in identifying city-owned vacant parcels with no development plans in order to offload them — particularly small slivers — back onto the tax rolls, potentially by selling to adjacent property owners. Other members raised questions about contamination (noting 1300 Cleveland is known to be contaminated), how the city acquired the parcels, and whether some listed as 'vacant' are actually serving purposes such as water retention. The committee agreed to bring the item back at the next meeting with a refined, narrowed list removing parcels already slated for development or serving active purposes, and directed staff to consult with Eric and Randy on contamination status.

discussions.item: Fall Leaf Collection Operations and Future Contracts
discussions.body: Alder Slansky raised constituent confusion about multiple leaf pickup rounds; Public Works staff member Dustin appeared and explained the city guarantees one full pass through the city with a baler, with follow-up vac trucks and sweepers that residents misinterpret as additional scheduled collections. Dustin noted complaints were actually down this year after consolidating to a single-phase map. The committee learned that all relevant contracts — tractor/baler, bale hauling, and yard waste — are expiring, and the current farmer-partner does not want to renew; the city may need to lease-to-own a baler. Alder Wiskowski raised the possibility of reducing or modifying leaf collection given the roughly $400,000–$500,000 annual cost, while Alder Martin cautioned that leaf collection helps reduce phosphorus and total dissolved solids discharging into the Wisconsin River under the TMDL requirements. Staff also explained that to earn DNR leaf credits, the city would need three to four collection rounds per neighborhood and an ordinance prohibiting leaves in the roadway — requirements currently unmet. The committee agreed to bring leaf collection back as a full agenda item in January, including contract options, communication improvements, service level expectations, and sustainability considerations.

discussions.item: Agenda Packet Timeline Update
discussions.body: Administration staff, led by what appears to be the county administrator and County Clerk Kim, presented an update on the agenda and packet preparation process, describing it as functioning like an agenda management system without dedicated software. Supervisor Rosemarie praised the current system, saying it was a marked improvement over past practices at other entities she had experienced.

discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson raised concerns about receiving packet materials too late — only by 8:00 a.m. on Friday mornings — saying that as a standing committee chair, he sometimes reviews memos and concludes items are 'not ready for prime time' but lacks time to act on that before the meeting. He asserted that policy-setting committee chairs, not administration, should be primary in setting agendas. The administrator acknowledged the feedback and noted that historically packet items were distributed in paper with no advance chair review, and that accommodating earlier chair review of packets would require reworking the current timeline and potentially the board rules.

It was noted that this may also require revisions to board rules. No action was taken; the item was informational only, and Supervisor Robinson was jokingly suggested as a task force chair on the topic.

overview: The Marathon County Board Executive Committee held a wide-ranging meeting covering the Bugtussle bond default crisis, the Hub City Wind Farm joint development agreement, a county road funding policy, and strategic plan updates. The committee voted unanimously to enter closed session to discuss strategy related to Bugtussle's failure to make payments on a $25 million conduit bond, leaving the county on the hook for a $347,409 shortfall, and also agreed to call a special full board meeting for the following Tuesday at 6 p.m. to address both the Alliant/Hub City Wind JDA response and the Bugtussle situation.

discussions.body: Two speakers addressed the committee. Joe Bergen of the Town of Day criticized the Alliant/Hub City Wind Farm proposed Joint Development Agreement (JDA) as vague and one-sided, noting provisions such as 90-day complaint response windows and unspecified haul routes, and urged the county to disregard the JDA and draft its own protective agreement. Ed Ruschinski, town chairman of Bergen, spoke about Moon Road, which accesses Big Oplain Park, arguing that the town maintains the road without property tax revenue from the park and requesting county funding assistance; he also suggested the county consider a user fee for horse trailer use on trails.

discussions.item: Strategic Plan Development Update and Next Steps
discussions.body: Vice Chair Boots reported that the 20 draft strategic objectives had been sent to the public and returned, with compilation planned for November and an informational packet expected for the December executive meeting. Staff discussed potentially adding data points for every strategy, not just each objective, which may push final adoption to January or February 2027. Approximately 150 public responses were received.

discussions.item: Comprehensive Revision to Ordinances to Reference Fee Schedule
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard briefly described the proposal to remove specific fee dollar amounts from ordinances and reference the newly adopted fee schedule instead. Supervisor Robinson raised concerns that some items — including Children with Disabilities Educational Board compensation, Civil Service Commission pay, vehicle registration fees, and statutorily set delinquent property tax percentages — were not appropriate for this process. Administration agreed to provide a redlined version and the committee voted unanimously to postpone action to the December executive committee meeting.

discussions.item: County Policy Regarding Funding of Town Roadways Providing Access to County Facilities (Moon Road and Duncan Road)
discussions.body: Deputy Administrator Homan and Director Pauley presented updates to a 2015 resolution governing county assistance to towns for roads accessing county parks and forest units, including two newly proposed additions: a section of Moon Road (Town of Bergen to Big Oplain Park) and Leather Camp Drive (Town of Bavent). Extensive debate followed on where to draw policy lines, particularly regarding highway facilities like the Kronenwetter salt shed and whether the resolution should expand beyond parks and forests. Supervisor Greiner supported gathering traffic count data specifically for Moon Road given its unique situation as the only county park with this access issue. Supervisor Boots, Robinson, and Ritter expressed caution about expanding scope without more research. The committee voted unanimously to postpone to no later than the January executive committee meeting, with administration directed to gather maps, traffic count methodology, historical cost data since 2015, information on peer county practices, any legal requirements for such a policy, existing township road agreements, and tonnage impacts from forestry operations.

discussions.item: Item 6D: Alliant/Hub City Wind JDA and Special Board Meeting
discussions.body: Chair Gibbs explained that Marathon County Resolution 5526 required the Alliant/Hub City Wind proposed JDA to be brought before the full board. He proposed calling a special board meeting the following Tuesday at 6 p.m. to allow all 38 board members to weigh in on a response — whether further negotiation, revision, or termination of discussions. The committee reached consensus on Tuesday evening and Gibbs said he would notify all board members to reserve that date.

discussions.item: Bugtussle Relationship Update and Discussion of Special Board Meeting
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard recapped the Bugtussle bond default: Bugtussle failed to deposit required funds into the debt service fund by October 15, received default notices on October 26-27, and the trustee made a November 2 payment from reserves. Bugtussle has failed to replenish the fund, leaving a shortfall of $347,409.01 that the county must pay under its guarantee by April 8, 2027. The county's annual obligation on the $25 million conduit issuance runs approximately $1,504,443 per year through 2051. The committee voted unanimously by roll call to enter closed session under Wisconsin Statutes 19.85(1)(e) and 19.85(1)(g) to discuss asset recovery strategy and potential litigation without revealing the county's hand to Bugtussle.

Ed Ruschinski, town chairman of Bergen, requested county funding assistance for Moon Road, which accesses Big Oplain Park, arguing the town receives no property tax from the park's roughly 900 acres in Bergen despite heavy road traffic, and suggested the county consider a horse trailer user fee for park trails.

overview: The Wausau City Council held its regular meeting on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, taking up proclamations for Homelessness Awareness Month, Hmong New Year, and Veterans Day, then approving the 2027 City of Wausau budget on a 7-4 vote after rejecting an amendment to use reserves to achieve net-zero new borrowing. The council also unanimously approved the consent agenda, which included designating Yawkey Park as a local historic landmark, and passed several other resolutions including the 2027 comprehensive fee schedule and a police Beat Patrol grant acceptance under suspension of the rules.

discussions.item: City Administrator Presentation
discussions.body: Mayor Diny presented an update on the city administrator proposal, noting a public information session drew 45 residents and an ongoing resident survey had received 296 responses with a week remaining. He argued that a city administrator model—adoptable by simple ordinance—would provide continuity, professional management, and separation of politics from day-to-day operations, and asked the council to retain the $150,000 budget line for the position. Alder Tierney questioned the cost estimates, noting uncertainty in the figures, while Alder Hoenecke expressed skepticism that adding an administrator would tangibly address residents' concerns about spending and performance. Alder Neal called the $150,000 figure insufficiently supported and said the audit should come first; Alder Wiskowski asked that multiple models—including a chief-of-staff option—be presented at a future committee of the whole. No vote was taken; the mayor indicated a committee-of-the-whole session would follow.

discussions.body: Alder Lukens requested a minor amendment to clarify that she had not objected but merely had a question during a prior item regarding the Flock camera resolution. A motion to amend was made by Lukens and seconded by Hoenecke; it passed on a voice vote. The amended minutes were then approved 11-0.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Four residents addressed the council. Two speakers focused on Flock license-plate-reader cameras, urging the council to send written termination notice to Flock by November 15 under contract Section 11.16, to omit Flock payments from the 2027 and 2028 budgets, and noting that 42 Wisconsin agencies had already ended or decided to end Flock contracts with no known litigation. One speaker read a statement from Yawkey heirs expressing full support for designating Yawkey Park as a historic landmark. A fourth speaker supported both the Yawkey Park landmarking and the city audit while expressing opposition to advancing a city administrator position without a referendum.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda
discussions.body: The consent agenda was moved by Neal and seconded by Slonski and passed unanimously 11-0. Mayor Diny specifically noted that the designation of Yawkey Park as a local historic landmark was included, calling out that it had passed unanimously through the Plan Commission and Historic Preservation Commission.

discussions.item: 2027 City of Wausau Budget Adoption
discussions.body: The budget came out of the Finance Committee 4-1. Alder Hoenecke moved an amendment to use general fund reserves to offset new borrowing so that net new debt would be zero (borrowing $18 million rather than $22 million); Finance Director Groat cautioned against it, noting Wausau's unassigned fund balance as a share of expenses was already on the lower end compared to peer cities, and recommended waiting until year-end. Alder Martens and Slonski also opposed the amendment, with Slonski citing the city's fund-balance policy limiting reserve draws to unanticipated, non-recurring needs; the amendment failed 2-9. On the main motion, Alder Wiskowski, Trueblood, and Lukens voiced concerns about the budget process, lack of broader public deliberation, and unresolved structural issues like a $1.368 million motor pool shortfall. Alder Martens, chair of Finance, summarized key amendments—reclassifying $150,000 from city administrator to audit, eliminating $50,000 for Flock, $45,000 for alley paving, $20,000 for trail planning, and $150,000 for downtown traffic redesign engineering—and noted 60% of the tax increase stems from fully funding 12 new firefighter-paramedics approved by April referendum. The budget was adopted 7-4, with an estimated $71.52 increase per $200,000 assessed home value.

discussions.item: Suspension of Rules and Beat Patrol Grant
discussions.body: The council voted 9-2 to suspend Rule 1D to allow late-arriving committee business. Under suspension, the council took up a Finance Committee resolution accepting a Wisconsin DOJ 2027 Beat Patrol Grant of $121,434 for the police department, which had passed Finance 5-0. Police Chief explained the grant has been received since 2019, is non-competitive but annual, and effectively funds approximately two officers; if lost, a difficult staffing conversation with the council would follow. Alder Hoenecke raised concern about vulnerability to federal funding changes and the lateness of the grant award relative to budget planning; the resolution passed 11-0.

discussions.body: A Finance Committee resolution approving the 2027 operating plan for Business Improvement District No. 1 downtown, which had passed Finance 5-0, was moved by Watson and seconded by Hoenecke. No discussion was recorded and it passed unanimously 11-0.

One speaker, the assistant director of the Leigh Yawkey Woodson Art Museum appearing in a professional capacity, read a statement from Yawkey heirs supporting designation of Yawkey Park as a historic landmark. A fourth resident, who identified herself as Christine Martins of Arthur Street, also spoke in support of the Yawkey Park landmarking and noted the letter from the Yawkey heirs had been read at every relevant meeting. A fifth resident (who spoke during the budget public hearing) expressed support for the audit over the city administrator proposal and said a survey was not sufficient substitute for a referendum on the administrator question.

overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held its annual budget meeting on November 10, 2026, to adopt the 2027 budget and property tax levy. After debating four amendments — including a failed $1.75 million levy reduction, a passed Flock camera funding reallocation, a passed $250,000 legal fund for wind farm and broadband litigation, and a passed pathologist fee schedule update — the board approved the amended 2027 budget. The board also unanimously appointed Lee Peek to fill the District 9 supervisory seat vacated by the resignation of Supervisor Chantel Foot.

discussions.item: Consent agenda items C8–C13B
discussions.body: Supervisor Straub pulled item C13C for a separate vote. The remaining consent agenda items C8 through C13B were approved unanimously on a motion by Supervisor Dreybeck, seconded by Supervisor Joong.

discussions.item: C13C — Authorizing sale of tax deeded property (Resolution 77-26)
discussions.body: Supervisor Straub argued against selling the property for $1, contending it was worth $25,000–$45,000 and that the county could demolish the mold-infested structure cheaply. Supervisor Robinson defended the sale, explaining the property was appraised at zero by a certified appraiser due to heavy mold infestation, that the city would demolish it and return it to the housing market, and that it relieved the county of a hazard. The motion to approve the $1 sale passed, but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: D14A — ATV/UTV ordinance on Highway 34 (Ordinance 53-26)
discussions.body: Supervisor Hoppa raised safety concerns about lighting on the bridge; the Highway Commissioner confirmed no additional lighting would be installed but that ATVs are required to have headlights and taillights, and that signage would be posted at route entry and exit points. Supervisor Neisath expressed concern about the 55 mph speed limit for slow-moving UTVs but was told speed limits on the state road are state-controlled. Supervisor Mask encouraged support. The ordinance passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Amendment 5 — $1.75 million levy reduction
discussions.body: Supervisor Sandelski moved to reduce the proposed tax levy increase by $1.75 million, arguing the county's healthy fund balances and investment returns made the 8% increase 'egregious.' Administrator Leonard and Supervisor Robinson countered that highway fund reserves are nearly fully committed, that the levy strategy is the least costly way to fund the $25 million highway shop shortfall without new borrowing, and that deferring the amount would simply shift it to next year's levy. Supervisors Dickinson and Straub supported the amendment, while Vice Chair Boes and Robinson urged rejection. After debate was closed by a two-thirds vote, the amendment was defeated.

discussions.item: Amendment 1 — Flock camera funding ($6,300); Amendment to Amendment — remove from levy instead of contingency
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson moved to transfer $6,300 for Flock automatic license plate reader cameras from the Sheriff's budget to the HR Finance contingency fund, pending policy discussions on data retention, access, auditing, and oversight. Supervisor Neisath offered an amendment to instead remove the $6,300 from the levy entirely, citing Fourth Amendment concerns and the direction Wausau had already taken in discontinuing Flock. Supervisors Trapp, Sandelski, Lammer, Rosenberg, and Hart supported removing the cameras entirely; Supervisors Kraebber, Robinson, Johnson, and Hoppa argued for keeping the tool with added oversight. The amendment to the amendment (levy reduction) failed; the original Amendment 1 (move to contingency) passed but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: Amendment 2 — $250,000 legal fund for Hub City Wind/Bug Tussle
discussions.body: Supervisor Jensen moved to increase the sales tax revenue estimate by $250,000 and place that amount in the administrator's special projects budget for legal expenses related to potential PSC intervention in the Alliant Hub City Wind project and potential Bug Tussle litigation. The HR Finance Committee had broadened the amendment beyond wind intervention alone. Administrator Leonard noted the board would need to authorize any actual expenditure. Supervisor Lammer asked how spending would be managed before final sales tax receipts are known, and was reassured by working capital practices. The amendment passed but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: Amendment 3 — Pathologist travel fee schedule
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson moved adoption of Amendment 3, which creates separate billing rates for pathologist travel time when testifying in civil and criminal cases — set at half the professional testifying rate, billed in 15-minute increments. The amendment had passed unanimously out of HR Finance Committee. After clarifying questions from Supervisors Krebs, Zhong, and Dickinson, the amendment passed but was not unanimous.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget — final vote as amended
discussions.body: Finance Director Sam presented the revised budget figures incorporating all passed amendments, bringing the total budget to $238,881,841. The board then voted to adopt the 2027 budget and property tax levy as amended; the motion carried but was not unanimous. Supervisor Robinson publicly thanked administration and the finance director for their work and encouraged board members to communicate legislative barriers to the administrator and leadership.

discussions.item: Appointment of Lee Peek to District 9 supervisory vacancy
discussions.body: Board Chair Gibbs thanked outgoing Supervisor Chantel Foot for nearly three years of service and noted her resignation effective midnight. The chair, vice chair, and clerk had interviewed three of four applicants. Supervisor Cavelli moved and Supervisor Krebs seconded the appointment of Lee Peek, a former county board member who served as vice chair in 2014 and 2016. Peek addressed the board, citing his prior service and familiarity with county issues. The appointment was approved unanimously and Peek was immediately sworn in.

publicComment: No public comment was offered at this meeting. However, Supervisor Robinson referenced public input from the prior week's budget hearing, specifically concerns raised by a named citizen (Mr. Gallo) regarding the Flock license plate reader program, which informed Amendment 1. Supervisor Trapp read aloud from a November 2026 investigative article by the Wausau Pilot and Review regarding the Flock program, citing concerns about the number of agencies with access to Marathon County's Flock data, audit practices, and data-sharing policies.

The most significant debate centered on the fire department equipment purchase totaling $214,521, with disagreement over how future payments would be funded before the item ultimately passed 4-1.

She expressed support for the committee's prior 5-0 vote to remove a $50,000 Flock Safety camera payment from the 2027 budget and move it to motor pool expenses. She urged the committee to request a written opinion from the city attorney confirming that the next Flock invoice belongs to the 2027 budget and that the city can exit the contract under Section 11.16 without penalty, and asked that written notice be sent to Flock by November 15 to terminate the contract before a December invoice is generated.

discussions.item: Revised Salary Structure for General Employees (Joint HR/Finance)
discussions.body: Human Resources staff presented a proposed 3% cost-of-living increase to the wage scale for non-represented general employees and seasonals, citing a 4.2% CPI-U increase and a 3.6% Social Security COLA. The presenter noted this is consistent with negotiated increases for transit (3.5% in 2026, 3% in 2027) and below the 4% increases for police and fire in 2027. Both the HR and Finance committees voted to approve without notable opposition; Alder Larson moved for HR and Alder Killion seconded; a separate motion carried for Finance.

discussions.item: Sole Source Request — Zoll Monitors and Ventilators for Fire Department
discussions.body: EMS Division Chief Matt O'Mullen presented a sole-source request totaling $214,521 for new cardiac monitors (reaching end of 8-year service life) and ventilators (over 15 years old with no available maintenance). He argued that purchasing both together before an April 2027 price increase saved approximately $40,000 through grouped pricing, avoided warranty costs, and trade-in value, with the first year's payment (~$40,000) covered by FAP (Fire Ambulance Program) funds. Alder Tierney questioned why the item was not in the 2027 budget and expressed reluctance to support it without a commitment to use FAP dollars in future years. Alder Hanke moved an amendment requiring 15% of subsequent four annual payments to come from FAP, but it was withdrawn after Alder Neal argued the payment structure was separate from the sole-source approval. A further amendment to strike payment language from the motion passed 4-1 (Tierney opposed), and the amended sole-source request then passed 4-1 with Tierney opposed. The committee acknowledged a financing agreement with Zoll would need to return to committee and council.

discussions.body: The committee approved the 2027 operating plan for BID No. 1, the downtown River District, with no notable discussion. Alder Watson moved, Alder Neal seconded, and it passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 2027 Beat Patrol Grant for Wausau Police Department
discussions.body: The committee approved the recurring Beat Patrol Grant for the police department. Alder Watson asked where the $40,000 city match would come from and was told it is already included in the 2027 budget. Watson then moved to approve; Alder Neal seconded; passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Budget Amendment for 2027 Lead Service Line Safe Drinking Water Award
discussions.body: Finance Director Mary Ann presented last-minute changes to the lead service line funding: anticipated principal forgiveness dropped from $7.9 million to just under $5 million, and the utility loan rate increased from 0.25% to 2.585% due to program competitiveness statewide, increasing net city borrowing by approximately $1.5 million on the homeowner side and $1.95 million on the utility side. Alder Neal moved to approve and Alder Watson seconded, but Watson withdrew her second after expressing concern that the committee had insufficient time to analyze the changes. Without a second, the motion died. The underlying budget figures already approved remain in place, and the amendment can be reintroduced when the financial assistance agreement from the DNR comes back to committee.

discussions.body: The committee approved the annual payment in lieu of taxes from Wausau Water Works with no substantive discussion. Alder Watson moved, Alder Neal seconded, passed unanimously.
