discussions.body: Finance Director Mary Ann explained the amendment covers projected year-end shortfalls, primarily in the motor pool (including $470,000 for the police department) and refuse/recycling fuel surcharges. Offsetting revenues include approximately $527,000 in additional SAFER grant income, crossing guard salary savings, and additional investment income. The net budget adjustment was estimated at approximately $1.3 million. Alder Hanke moved, Alder Watson seconded, and it passed unanimously.

overview: The Marathon County Public Safety Committee held its November 2026 meeting focused heavily on the Sheriff's Office's Flock automatic license plate reader (ALPR) program, with significant public input and committee debate over data privacy, oversight, and whether to defund the cameras. The committee also received presentations on the Sheriff's Office drone program and a 2027 budget overview. No formal votes were taken at the committee level, though a budget amendment moving $6,300 in Flock funding to a contingency fund was noted as pending a full County Board vote that evening.

discussions.item: Approval of September 8th and October 6th, 2026 Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: One supervisor objected to approving the minutes, alleging that his request to place Flock cameras on the October agenda was deflected off-camera by Administrator Lance Leonard, and that this was not captured in the record. The clerk explained that minutes only capture motions and actions, with video timestamps serving as the official record. The chair noted that Lance Leonard helps set agendas and that is why members are referred to him. The objecting supervisor refused to approve the minutes; the motion carried over his objection with the majority voting aye, though no specific tally was stated.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget Overview - Flock ALPR Funding
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson (referred to by others) explained that the Human Resources Finance and Property Committee had reviewed an amendment to move $6,300 budgeted for Flock cameras into a contingency fund, contingent on resolving concerns about access, oversight, and data retention. County Administrator Lance Leonard and Corporation Counsel Brian [inaudible] clarified that the county board cannot directly control sheriff's operational contracts due to the sheriff's status as a constitutional officer, creating a legal gray area. Committee members questioned whether pulling funding would actually force cameras down and whether future contracts would require board approval; both questions were left largely unresolved pending further legal analysis.

discussions.item: Sheriff's Office Drone Program
discussions.body: Sheriff Chad Bileb presented the drone program, noting the office operates three types of drones used for crash investigations, search and rescue, building clearing, and community events. The team includes approximately seven members, with three or four Part 107 FAA-certified pilots. Captain Seibert was present to answer technical questions. Committee members asked about recreational drone pilots potentially assisting or interfering with law enforcement operations; the sheriff indicated legal liability and HR concerns would preclude using volunteer pilots, and that recreational operators are not required to submit footage unless legally compelled.

discussions.item: Flock ALPR Contract Update and Committee Discussion
discussions.body: Sheriff Bileb addressed the committee's previously submitted questions: the office contracts for eight Falcon ALPR cameras funded by Wisconsin DOJ grants, plus two operated for the Village of Rib Mountain; cameras are located on I-39 and State Highway 29; early termination costs are $500 per camera. The sheriff acknowledged that up to 1,580 agencies have sharing access and that, following feedback from Felix Gallo, Captain Stefanik is auditing and significantly reducing that list. The sheriff maintained that Marathon County does not subscribe to Flock's traffic analytics product and that raw data is deleted after 30 days, but acknowledged disagreement with Gallo on what the contract's perpetual license covers. Multiple supervisors and non-committee county board members spoke against the program, citing mass surveillance concerns, Fourth Amendment issues, and lack of independent oversight, while supervisors Hoppa and one other expressed support or ambivalence, noting real public safety benefits. Sheriff Bileb stated he would not voluntarily remove the cameras, and indicated he expects state legislation on ALPR to emerge in the upcoming session.

publicComment: Felix Gallo of Highland Park in Wausau spoke during public comment, raising detailed concerns about the Flock ALPR contract's data retention terms. He argued that the contract's perpetual data license (sections 4, 5, and 6.6) survives termination and is not limited to 30 days, contradicting the sheriff's office memo. He warned that images can be downloaded by thousands of external agencies during the first 30 days and retained indefinitely, and that so-called 'de-identified' aggregate data can be used by Flock for future products. He also flagged that the office was not auditing searches by the 1,500-plus external agencies with access. Additionally, Supervisor David Nyceath of District 21 (not a committee member) spoke at length during the Flock discussion, urging the committee to defund the cameras, citing Fourth Amendment concerns, risk of data breaches, mission creep, and the precedent set by Wausau's 9-1 vote to cover its cameras. Supervisor Joel [inaudible] read aloud a citizen group statement summarizing a Wausau Pilot and Review investigative report alleging discrepancies between what the sheriff told supervisors and what the office's own records and policies show.

title: Human Resources, Finance & Property Committee Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Human Resources, Finance & Property Committee met on Monday, November 9, 2026, to consider amendments to the 2027 budget and property tax levy resolution ahead of the full county board meeting. The committee approved three of four proposed budget amendments — including redirecting $6,300 budgeted for automated license plate readers into a committee contingency fund, adding $250,000 in projected sales tax revenue earmarked for legal costs related to wind energy intervention and broadband litigation, and updating the medical examiner fee schedule — while voting not to recommend a $3.5 million reduction in capital improvement funding. The levy resolution was forwarded to the full board for adoption.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Three members of the public spoke. The first, a former supervisor, urged the committee to use the opioid settlement fund — currently holding approximately $2.5 million with another $3.7 million expected — to offset opioid-related county expenses rather than relying on the tax levy. The second speaker, identifying himself as an engineer and finance professional, presented a spreadsheet he had emailed to committee members and administrator Leonard, arguing that phasing in the North Central Healthcare transfer to debt levy over two years would result in $3 million less in taxes while still maintaining adequate reserves; he recommended taking $2 million of the $3.5 million and applying it to the debt levy. A third speaker urged the committee to pause Flock license plate reader funding, citing concerns about mass surveillance, broad data sharing with over a thousand entities, ICE searches, and inadequate data security, and invited committee members to visit unflockwausau.org/marathon.

discussions.item: Amendment 1: Automated License Plate Reader (Flock) Funding
discussions.body: Chair Robinson introduced Amendment 1, which would transfer the $6,300 budgeted for Flock automated license plate readers from the sheriff's department budget into the HR/Finance/Property Committee contingency fund, to be released only by a vote of the committee. Supervisor Nath stated he preferred stripping the funds entirely from the budget and returning them to the levy rather than placing them in a contingency fund. Vice Chair Pool raised concerns about the amendment limiting the sheriff's flexibility on data sharing, particularly for public safety matters involving ICE and human trafficking, and said he would not support it without changes. Chair Robinson clarified that a separate resolution would need to be adopted addressing data retention, access, and audit policies, and noted a productive morning meeting had occurred with the administrator, sheriff, and others. Kurt Gibbs moved to transfer the $6,300 to committee contingency; the motion passed but was not unanimous, with Supervisor Nath voting no.

discussions.item: Amendment 2: Sales Tax Revenue Increase for Legal Services
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard explained that Amendment 2, authored by Supervisor Jensen who was absent, would increase projected sales tax revenues by $250,000 and place a corresponding appropriation in the administrator's special projects cost center for legal services, primarily intended for potential county intervention in a Public Service Commission proceeding related to the Hub City wind project. Kurt Gibbs expressed support but pushed to broaden the purpose to include litigation related to the county's broadband bond guarantee with Bug Tussle. Finance Director Fensky confirmed that if sales tax did not meet the increased projection, the designated legal funds would be allocated first before the surplus rolled to the non-EP departmental budget, and that historically the county budgets sales tax approximately 11.68% below Forward Analytics projections. Vice Chair Pool moved to approve the amendment; Gibbs seconded and successfully added a friendly amendment broadening the funds' use to cover intervention and other potential litigation. The motion passed but was not unanimous, with one member (identified as Cody) voting no.

discussions.item: Amendment 3: Medical Examiner Pathologist Travel Fee Schedule
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard presented a staff-initiated fee schedule amendment adding travel time fees for the pathologist testifying in civil and criminal cases, noting the existing testimony rate was already in the fee schedule but a travel rate had been overlooked during budget development. No significant revenue impact was anticipated. Kurt Gibbs agreed to sponsor the amendment; he moved to incorporate the new fees, seconded by Supervisor Nath, and the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Amendment 4: $3.5 Million Reduction in CIP/NCHC Transfer
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard and Finance Director Fensky explained that Amendment 4, submitted by Supervisor Sundelski who was not present, would reduce the North Central Healthcare revenue transfer to capital improvements by $3.5 million, redirecting it toward debt service. Kurt Gibbs and Vice Chair Pool voiced strong opposition, with Gibbs citing the county's $25 million commitment for the new highway shop, the approximately $37 million remaining liability from the Bug Tussle broadband bond guarantee, and the risk that a $1.5 million debt service obligation to Bug Tussle cannot legally be placed on the levy without additional borrowing. Administrator Leonard warned that reducing the CIP now would likely trade a tax cut today for a larger tax increase with interest later, and cited additional uncertainties including potential Act 10 changes, federal 'One Big Beautiful Bill' Medicaid impacts, ARPA expiration, and reduced investment income as $55 million leaves the investment portfolio. Gibbs moved that the committee not recommend Amendment 4; the motion passed but was not unanimous, with Vice Chair Pool voting no, stating he wished to remain neutral.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget and Property Tax Levy Resolution
discussions.body: Finance Director Fensky walked the committee through Resolution 78-26, which sets the 2027 budget and property tax levy. She explained that the total budget was $238,631,841 and highlighted the breakdown of operational levy, special purpose levies for bridge/culvert aid and library (which are levy limit exceptions), debt levy, prior year unused levy adjustment, and state special charges. She noted the resolution already incorporated $50,000 in committee contingency funds, subject to change based on board amendments the following evening. Kurt Gibbs moved to approve and forward the resolution to the full board; the motion was seconded by Supervisor Sean and passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 28th Avenue Properties — Disposition
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard explained that properties acquired along 28th Avenue for a potential highway corridor relocation are no longer needed for that purpose after consultation with the City of Wausau and Village of Maine confirmed neither municipality wished to pursue the corridor realignment. He proposed listing developable parcels on Wisconsin Surplus, with any proceeds going back to the highway reserve and potentially applied to the highway shop project. Kurt Gibbs supported listing at minimum prices equal to fair market value. The committee reached consensus directing the administrator to return at a future meeting with a parcel-by-parcel overview including evaluation prices, developability assessments, and proposed courses of action, rather than taking a formal vote at this meeting.

discussions.item: Year-to-Date Budget Reports (through August 2026)
discussions.body: Finance Director Fensky reviewed August 2026 year-to-date reports, noting no major concerns. She flagged that the homeless shelter budget had been fully expended and would shift to contingency, that Clerk of Courts psychology evaluation fees were running high but expected to stay within budget, and that the social services consortia accounting and a working capital transfer from the social improvement fund would require budget amendments before year-end. Chair Robinson asked staff to investigate whether permit revenue in CPZ/zoning was trending down given lower-than-expected figures, and Fensky agreed to bring clarification to the next meeting. A loss in the investment allocation in April was noted as a temporary paper loss that had been recouped in subsequent months.

discussions.item: Other Business — Cherokee County Park Land Acquisition
discussions.body: Vice Chair Pool raised the previously approved acquisition of land adjacent to Cherokee County Park and suggested pausing the purchase to see whether the new state legislature would renew Knowles-Nelson Stewardship Program funding, which he said he now assessed at near-certainty. He proposed waiting approximately eight to ten months to potentially use Knowles-Nelson funds instead of county taxpayer funds, noting the land was not going anywhere. Chair Robinson acknowledged the suggestion and indicated the administration would take it under advisement, with no formal vote taken.

publicComment: Three members of the public spoke. A former supervisor spoke remotely, urging the committee to use the opioid settlement fund — holding approximately $2.5 million with $3.7 million more expected through 2038 — to offset opioid-related county expenses rather than taxing residents when substantial funds exist in reserve, suggesting up to $490,000 annually could be applied after retaining funds for jail treatment programs. A second speaker, who identified himself as an engineer and finance professional, presented a spreadsheet he emailed to committee members showing that phasing in the NCHC transfer over two years would reduce taxes by $3 million while maintaining reserves above policy minimums, and argued the county consistently over-budgets highway expenditures, making sound decision-making difficult; he recommended applying $2 million of the $3.5 million transfer to the debt levy. A third speaker urged the committee to pause Flock license plate reader funding, arguing the platform as implemented constitutes mass surveillance with 30-day data retention accessible to over a thousand entities across multiple states, that ICE has conducted searches through the system, and that officers have misused it; he outlined specific policy reforms and directed committee members to unflockwausau.org/marathon.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Finance Director John presented a detailed budget overview. Key highlights included a proposed assessed tax rate of $4.25 (equalized equivalent of $2.71), a total tax levy of approximately $2.9 million representing a 6.79% increase, no water or sewer rate increases, a garbage fee increase of $39.24 largely due to a diesel fuel surcharge, and a 3.5% COLA for non-elected positions. John noted the village's unassigned fund balance has grown from 3.52% in 2023 to approximately 34% for 2025, and previewed that a 2027 revaluation will likely drop the assessed tax rate significantly in 2028. Trustee Coyle thanked staff for presenting a 'competent budget,' implicitly referencing past budget shortfalls in 2023-2024 when debt service was underfunded by approximately $1.2 million over two years.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-013 - Adopt 2027 General Fund Operating Budget
discussions.body: Trustee Lesniak moved and Trustee Stowell seconded adoption of the 2027 general fund operating budget with a total appropriation of $6.5 million and a tax levy increase of 6.79%. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0 on roll call vote with no dissent or notable debate.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-014 - Adopt 2027 Budget for Debt Service, Special Revenue, Capital Projects, and Proprietary Funds
discussions.body: Trustee Stowell moved and Trustee Mishka seconded adoption of the resolution covering all other funds including debt service, special revenue, capital projects, TID districts, and utility funds. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0 on roll call with no discussion.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-015 - Adopt 2027 Capital Improvements Program Budget
discussions.body: Trustee Coyle moved and Trustee Solheim seconded adoption of the 2027 CIP budget totaling approximately $4.3 million, with proposed general obligation borrowing of roughly $1.865 million. John clarified that approving the CIP budget does not authorize immediate borrowing; separate borrowing resolutions must come before the board in 2027. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0.

discussions.item: Resolution 2026-016 - Appointment of Connie Nowak as Village Clerk
discussions.body: Trustee Mishka moved and Trustee Mortensen seconded appointing Connie Nowak as village clerk. Finance Director John flagged a potential error in the resolution's first 'whereas' clause, noting the charter ordinance specifies April as the start of the term rather than October; the board agreed to accept an abbreviated appointment now and clean up the language consistent with charter requirements. Multiple trustees praised Nowak, with Joling noting residents had already given her positive feedback. The resolution passed unanimously 7-0.

discussions.item: Legal Services Agreement with Wolfram, Gamoke and Hutchinson
discussions.body: Trustee Mortensen moved and Trustee Solheim seconded approval of the legal services agreement. Brief discussion noted the contract is essentially the same as the existing one and that Village Attorney Wolfram has been well regarded, including by the former police chief. The agreement passed unanimously 7-0.

discussions.item: Future Agenda Items
discussions.body: Village Administrator Jim raised the possibility of moving from two board meetings per month to one meeting per month on the fourth Monday, framing it as a way to streamline committee-to-board workflow and reduce scheduling burdens on trustees. He noted an ordinance change would be required and indicated it would be a discussion item at the next meeting. Discussion also touched on the rationale for Friday afternoon office closures, with staff explaining that uninterrupted time is needed for meeting minutes and audit tasks, and that a deputy clerk hire is planned for late first quarter 2027.

publicComment: One public speaker, identified as Bernie, addressed the board during the public hearing on the 2027 budget. He commented on the state levy limit worksheet and debt service adjustment figures, challenged the accuracy of per-capita tax comparisons between Kronenwetter (317 per capita, 84% residential) and commercial-heavy communities like Schofield (39% residential), questioned the proposed deputy clerk position given the village's Friday afternoon office closure policy, and criticized the village ethics committee as 'totally meaningless' and unworkable. No other members of the public spoke.

overview: The Village of Weston Public Works Committee held its regular meeting on November 10, 2026, covering a detailed infiltration and inflow (I&I) study presentation for the Rothschild sewer basin, a sewer rate increase recommendation, and approvals of several intergovernmental agreements and design contracts. Key decisions included recommending Option F for 2027 sewer rates, approving a pedestrian crossing design contract at County Trunk X and Sternberg Avenue, approving a storm pond construction agreement, and approving an intergovernmental agreement with the Town of Weston for Ross Avenue reconstruction.

discussions.item: I&I Study Presentation
discussions.body: Sean Dudy of Inpipe Technology presented results of a 44-day infiltration and inflow study covering approximately 26,000 feet of sewer pipe in the Rothschild area south of Highway 29. The study identified two 'red' priority areas — basin 2 and basin 3 — totaling about 3,300 feet, where groundwater infiltration and rain-driven inflow were highest, with one area showing 500-600% flow increases during rain events. Staff noted they had already identified a low manhole in one hot spot and discussed potential slip lining as a remediation tool. Committee members asked about flow volumes (approximately 1.9 to 5 gallons per minute in problem areas) and whether CCTV inspection had been done; staff confirmed historical televising exists but has not yet targeted these specific areas. Staff framed the study as providing data-driven direction to focus limited maintenance dollars rather than treating the entire neighborhood.

discussions.item: VIP (Village Improvement Projects) Update
discussions.body: Public Works Director Michael provided updates on numerous active projects: Weston A special assessments are expected for the board next Monday; Scullfield A has concrete work remaining for spring 2027 with Treweiler as subcontractor; Bladl Avenue final paving is complete; Concord and Bayberry paving began the morning of the meeting; Ross Avenue Metro to Alderson project is targeted for February bid; Fuller Street punch list work was completed. The Ross Avenue and County Road X design contract (item 14) was previewed, with committee members raising concerns about insurance and liability limitation language in the consultant contract. Staff confirmed they would align the contract with the village's standard attorney-reviewed template before board execution.

discussions.item: Street Operations Update
discussions.body: Staff reported completion of storm sewer work at wells 7 and 8 near the golf course, reconstruction of the outfall structure at Kathy Street including a new trash guard to prevent children from entering the pipe, overlay of Heron Street's northbound lane using a combination of contracted RC Pavers equipment and village-hauled asphalt, and replacement of a culvert on Harney Avenue. Fall curbside yard waste and leaf pickup operations were described as requiring at least four DPW staff members daily, with vac trucks averaging 10 loads each at 20 cubic yards per load. A committee member asked staff to quantify the cost savings from using in-house labor alongside contracted paving services; staff agreed to compile those figures for the December meeting, noting two competing bids differed by about $15,000.

discussions.item: 2027 Sanitary Sewer Rate Policy Discussion and Recommendation
discussions.body: Staff presented updated rate options following the previous month's discussion, noting that simply breaking even (Option A) was not considered viable by committee members. Discussion centered on Options G (projected net income ~$160,000) and F (projected net revenue ~$113,000). One member noted that at average usage of 12,000 gallons per year, the difference between G and F is roughly $5 per quarter or $20 per year per household. Committee members cited the need for funds to support slip lining projects, rising Mountain Metro treatment costs (up nearly $800,000 since 2019), and aging infrastructure including 10 miles of asbestos water main. The committee voted to recommend Option F, with staff noting rates could be lowered in future years if significant surplus developed.

discussions.item: Sidewalk Snow Removal Policy
discussions.body: Discussion was prompted by a resident letter from someone abutting Fuller Street who is handicapped and cannot clear their sidewalk. Committee members unanimously agreed that creating an individual exception would be unworkable and set a problematic precedent, with one member stating 'if you don't follow it, you just don't even have one really.' The committee voted to make no substantive change to the snow removal policy but directed staff to update the written policy to reflect current actual practices, including newly added paths not previously listed. One member suggested the village newsletter could solicit volunteer 'sidewalk angels' to assist residents in need; staff agreed to include that in the newsletter.

discussions.item: County Trunk X and Sternberg Avenue Pedestrian Design Contract
discussions.body: Staff explained the village did not receive the TAP (Transportation Alternatives Program) grant it had applied for, meaning pedestrian crossing improvements at County Trunk X and Sternberg Avenue — identified in the West Elementary School Safe Routes to School plan — would now be fully at village expense, estimated at $150,000-$200,000 construction cost with a design fee around $45,000. The improvements include a refuge island and pedestrian-activated warning lights. The committee voted to recommend awarding the design contract, contingent on staff reviewing and aligning the consultant's liability limitation language with the village's standard contract template before execution.

discussions.item: Business 51 Storm Pond Construction Intergovernmental Agreement
discussions.body: Staff presented a construction-phase intergovernmental agreement for the Highway 29/Business 51 storm water pond shared with the Village of Rothschild and City of Schofield. Staff noted updated hydraulic modeling now shows the pond will remove 225 pounds of phosphorus annually — nearly double the originally estimated 122 pounds — which will delay the need for additional phosphorus removal projects. The village's cost share percentage increases slightly as a result, but staff framed this as favorable overall. The committee voted to recommend the village board approve the agreement.

discussions.item: Ross Avenue/Town of Weston Intergovernmental Agreement
discussions.body: Staff presented a draft intergovernmental agreement with the Town of Weston for reconstruction of Ross Avenue from Riverbend Road to Paula's Avenue, programmed for 2028 construction with a surface transportation grant covering approximately 75% of costs (over $2.2 million). The cost split is approximately 51% village and 49% town based on right-of-way analysis. The agreement includes annexation provisions so that if town land annexes to the village post-construction, the village would reimburse the town for its proportionate remaining debt payments. A committee member raised a question about whether driveways should be explicitly included in the annexation reimbursement language, and staff agreed to refine that language. The committee voted to recommend approval with possible minor clarifications on pre- and post-annexation cost provisions.

title: Rules Review Committee Meeting
committee: City of Wausau Rules Review Committee
overview: The Wausau Rules Review Committee held an organizational 'table-setting' session on November 9th to identify potential revisions to the City of Wausau's standing rules (Chapter 2.16 of municipal code). No formal votes or rule changes were made; the committee identified several areas for future revision including public comment procedures, standing committee appointments, absence notification, subcommittee chair elections, and the reporting chain from this committee to council. The committee agreed to reconvene in mid-January 2027 after members submit redlined proposed changes to the city attorney.

discussions.item: Reporting chain: committee of the whole vs. direct to council
discussions.body: Committee members, including Alder Tierney and Terry Kilian, questioned why recommendations must go to the committee of the whole before the full council, calling it redundant since the committee of the whole is essentially the same body. City Attorney Vinnie confirmed the reporting structure was set by the resolution creating this subcommittee. Mayor Doug Diny suggested the committee of the whole step allows all alders to weigh in on rule changes before council action. No formal change was made; it was noted the resolution could be amended via suspension of the rules at a future council meeting.

discussions.item: Rule 16 - public comment engagement policy
discussions.body: The chair raised whether the existing practice of not engaging with public commenters should be codified in the rules, prompted by recent media coverage. Alder Hanei argued the current practice was proper and warned against a 'knee-jerk reaction to a mischaracterization by a media outlet.' Terry Kilian said a brief response to a direct question from a commenter could be respectful and appropriate. Alder Tierney raised concerns about managing time and consistency in contentious situations. Mayor Diny noted responses have historically been limited to procedural direction from the chair, and that the practice only became controversial after media reported on it. No rule change was finalized; members were asked to submit proposed language.

discussions.item: Standing committee appointments - proposed rule addition
discussions.body: Alderperson Lou Larson raised during public comment that he and Alder Rasmussen were removed from long-held committee assignments, which he attributed to retribution. The chair noted two alders had requested a rule providing continuity for experienced alders in committee appointments. Alder Hanei and Terry Kilian both stated they were not in favor of changing the rule giving the mayor appointment authority, with Hanei noting it could undermine the mayor's prerogative and citing Marshfield's annual reappointment model as a possible alternative. No change was recommended.

discussions.item: Rule 13 - subcommittee chairs and executive committee chairperson
discussions.body: Alder Tierney argued subcommittees such as bike and pedestrian should elect their own chair and vice chair, consistent with how standing committees operate. Terry Kilian additionally questioned why the executive committee — a standing committee — is required by Rule 13H to be chaired by the council president rather than electing its own chair. The city attorney noted some boards and commissions are governed by statute and cannot be changed, but council standing committees and subcommittees are within the rules' scope. No formal change was made; proposed language would be drafted for the next meeting.

discussions.item: Suspension of rules and consent agenda efficiency
discussions.body: Alder Tierney expressed strong opposition to routine suspension of the rules, noting a previous rules committee under Gary Gelman had addressed the same recurring problem. Alder Hanei raised concerns about consent agendas containing items from committees some alders did not serve on, and suggested items that failed in committee should never appear on the consent agenda. Mayor Diny noted the old agenda software listed committee vote tallies alongside resolutions and suggested that practice be restored. The city attorney cited Rule 14 as already allowing committee chairs to give brief reports to council on their items. No rule changes were made; members encouraged to submit redlined proposals.

discussions.item: Number and structure of standing committees
discussions.body: Alder Hanei raised the question of whether the city has too many committees, noting items sometimes travel through multiple committees before reaching council. He suggested exploring whether fewer committees with more members could mean more efficient city business and broader aldermanic awareness of issues before council votes. The chair acknowledged this was raised by the mayor at the organizational meeting and said the door remains open for the committee to consider recommending structural changes. No action taken.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment: Lou Larson identified himself as the alderperson for District 10. He raised two concerns: first, that placing public comment before the meeting sets a negative tone and risks turning council meetings into 'all-night extravaganzas' when contentious topics draw large crowds; second, that experienced alders including himself and Alder Rasmussen were removed from long-held committee assignments this term, which he characterized as retribution for disagreements with the mayor.

overview: The Marathon County Infrastructure Committee met on November 5th, 2026 and took several significant actions, most notably approving an ordinance to allow ATV/UTV access on State Highway 34 and separately voting to request the state DOT approve flashing warning signs for that segment. The committee also received updates on the 2027 budget, the routine state highway maintenance agreement, the Wausau MPO long-range transportation plan, and IT department projects, though no votes were taken on those informational items.

discussions.item: Approval of October 1, 2026 Minutes
discussions.body: The minutes were approved without discussion. A motion was made by Watson and seconded by Coyle. The motion carried on a voice vote.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget Overview
discussions.body: County Administrator Leonard and HR/Finance/Property Committee Chair Robinson presented a brief overview, noting the deadline for proposed budget amendments was 8:00 a.m. the following morning for Finance Committee review before county board adoption. Robinson highlighted that one driver of budget growth is funding for the highway facility. No amendments were proposed and no votes were taken.

discussions.item: ATV/UTV Access on State Highway 34
discussions.body: Supervisor Gal raised safety concerns about ATV/UTV traffic mixing with high-volume truck traffic on State Highway 34, citing approximately 6,000 vehicles per day compared to the county's 1,500-vehicle threshold for county trunk highways, and noting that ATVs traveling at 35 mph would share the road with trucks doing 60 mph. Jeff Gates, a member of the public, stated that hundreds of riders would use the route and that the current detour adds roughly 25 minutes of travel time. DOT representative Mike Crutchmer confirmed the DOT reviewed the draft ordinance but noted he deferred to access engineer Rich Hendrick on specifics. Vice Chair Gal moved to approve the ordinance with a condition requiring flashing warning lights; Supervisor Dickinson argued the signage question was separate and moved to divide the question into two parts. After procedural discussion involving corporation counsel, the motion was split: the original ordinance was approved unanimously on a voice vote, and a separate motion requesting the state DOT approve flashing warning signage for the ATV route on State Highway 34 passed 5-2.

discussions.item: Safe Routes to School Program and Cronin Area Request
discussions.body: Commissioner Lang explained that Marathon County's historical practice is to co-sign Safe Routes to School applications rather than serve as the primary sponsor, as the primary benefit is local. He noted the next application window is fall 2027, and that North Central Regional Planning assists communities with applications. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Routine Maintenance Agreement Update
discussions.body: Commissioner Lang and DOT Operations Manager Mike Crutchmer reviewed the annual routine maintenance agreement under which Marathon County maintains state roads. Discussion focused on cost reimbursement concerns, particularly the dramatic increase in plow blade costs — from roughly $300 to $750 for a 3-foot blade — and the inadequacy of the 5-year rolling average reimbursement rate to keep pace. Supervisors Gal and Sybert asked for data on the county's overall financial partnership with the state. No vote was taken; staff was directed to gather reimbursement and cost-sharing figures.

discussions.item: MPO Long Range Transportation Plan Update
discussions.body: Staff member Lori presented the update, noting four roadway segments identified as Level of Service D: State Highway 153/Main Street between 4th and Old Highway 51, Bridge Street over the Wisconsin River, West Thomas Street between South 3rd and Cleveland Avenue, and Grand Avenue between Townline Road and Thomas Street. The draft plan will be released for public review later in November through December. No vote was taken.

discussions.item: CCIT Projects Update
discussions.body: CCIT Director Greg Klein highlighted open enrollment IT support for the city and county, an upgrade to NetMotion VPN software across 128 squad cars to meet new criminal justice encryption requirements, and ongoing transition of network support for the UWSP campus on River Drive ahead of a January 1st handoff. A question arose about the status of the former Marathon County Credit Union building on Thomas Street, with the administrator confirming the occupant has not yet vacated. No vote was taken.

overview: The Marathon County Joint Extension, Education, Economic Development and Human Resources, Finance, and Property Committees met to consider a one-year operating lease for the former UWSP campus theater building with the Marathon Center for Arts and Culture (MCAC), and to review two new proposals for the River Drive properties. The committees approved the MCAC lease with a modification requiring the tenant to cover approximately $7,428 in annual building insurance costs, then voted to enter closed session to discuss negotiation strategy on the River Drive RFP responses.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Two speakers offered public comment. Jim Davo, Village Administrator of Kronenwetter, thanked county staff in the clerk's office, highway shop, and sheriff's department for their professionalism and cooperative work with the village. Gail Marshall, speaking by phone, urged the committees to reject the current RFP proposals for the River Drive properties, arguing the process had failed to produce meaningful results and recommending the county instead hire a commercial real estate broker — estimating a 3% commission would still yield 97% of sale proceeds to taxpayers. She also asked what the county currently insures the River Drive properties for.

discussions.item: Approval of September 9, 2026 Joint Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: Minutes were approved by both committees in separate motions. For the Extension, Education, and Economic Development (Triple-ED) committee, Supervisor Hagen moved and the motion was seconded; it passed. For the HR, Finance, and Property (HRFC) committee, Vice Chair Pool moved and Supervisor Watson seconded; it passed.

discussions.item: UWSP Campus Redevelopment Update and MCAC One-Year Lease
discussions.body: Administrator Chris Holman reported that a city feasibility study agreement is in place, building systems are being inventoried and winterized, and staff are working with the UW exit committee. The proposed one-year operating lease with the Marathon Center for Arts and Culture (MCAC) was presented to bridge the gap while MCAC finalizes its 501c3 property tax exemption with the state. Tim Parker, CEO of the Community Foundation of North Central Wisconsin and MCAC fiscal agent, told committees that 95% of office spaces are leased and theater bookings are at 60% through June, with January and February already full. Kurt Gibbs raised the issue of insurance costs, noting the building is insured for approximately $13 million and the annual premium is roughly $7,428; he argued that cost should be borne by the tenant. Vice Chair Pool moved to approve the lease with a modification directing staff to negotiate inclusion of the $7,428 insurance cost spread over monthly payments; the motion was seconded and passed.

discussions.item: River Drive RFP Proposals – Raise and Roast Cafe (Oswald)
discussions.body: Justin and Elena Oswald presented their proposal to purchase 210 River Drive for $1 to develop 'Raise and Roast Cafe,' envisioning an affordable community cafe on the ground floor and a fundraising event venue on the second floor, with free recreational activities and partnerships with downtown institutions. Holman noted the proposal has strong alignment with criteria for activating unused property, community benefit, and local ownership, with moderate alignment on job creation and tax base reactivation. No formal vote or counter-offer was made in open session.

discussions.item: River Drive RFP Proposals – VFW Post 388 Veterans and Community Campus
discussions.body: Tamara Sillers, VFW Post 388 events coordinator, presented the VFW's proposal to acquire all three River Drive buildings (210, 212, and 326) to create a veterans and community campus, with 210 as an event venue, 212 as a community lounge with mental health counseling space and bingo, and 326 as garage and storage. She noted the VFW vacated River Drive around 2017 and the move was a mistake for community connectivity. Supervisors questioned how the new model differs from the bar-and-restaurant model that led to the prior departure, the organization's current revenue sources, and its nonprofit status (501c19). Holman disclosed the appraised market value of the River Drive parcel at $2,268,000 (land $87,000, improvements $1,261,000 as of November 2025) and insurance values: 210 at $2,635,700, 212 at $3,734,400, and 326 at $1,271,100. The presiding chair expressed disappointment at dollar-sale proposals given significant county investment, stating an obligation to taxpayers to maximize return.

discussions.item: Motion to Enter Closed Session on River Drive RFP
discussions.body: Corp Counsel explained that closed session was appropriate to discuss negotiation strategy and potential counter-proposals without revealing the county's position to the proposing parties. Both committees voted separately by roll call to enter closed session pursuant to Wisconsin Statute 19.85(1)(e) for competitive or bargaining reasons, specifically consideration of RFP responses for River Drive property. Both roll call votes passed unanimously.

overview: The Kronenwetter Plan Commission held its November 4, 2026 meeting primarily to deliberate and act on a conditional use permit for Eau Claire River LLC to operate an aggregate mine and pond expansion at 1320 Kowalski Road. After extensive discussion of operating conditions, noise, flood storage, and future development potential, the commission unanimously approved the CUP 7-0 with conditions. discussions.item: Conditional Use Permit - Eau Claire River LLC, 1320 Kowalski Road
discussions.body: The commission deliberated extensively on the CUP for an approximately 35.58-acre aggregate mining and pond expansion operation. Community Development Director Nathan Sandwick (referred to as 'Nathan' throughout) guided the commission through findings of fact and proposed conditions. Applicant representatives Tom and Gary provided extensive background on the site's history, flood storage engineering, prior interchange planning discussions, the settlement agreement with the Diocese that led to dropping a lawsuit, and confirmed no blasting or asphalt batching plant would occur. After working through roughly 14 proposed condition bullet points, the commission agreed to include conditions on: permitted hours of operation (6 a.m.–7 p.m. Monday–Friday, 6 a.m.–noon Saturday, year-round); a five-year renewal review period; perimeter staking of the excavation area; requiring trucks to be covered to suppress dust and debris; implementation of a reclamation plan; compliance with Village erosion and stormwater control standards; a geotechnical analysis by a qualified engineer to confirm excavation will not compromise adjacent roadways; and compliance with all applicable laws. Conditions on road repair monitoring, specific noise monitoring by either party, and redundant buffer yard language already covered by code were not included.

discussions.body: Following the vote, commissioners discussed scheduling a future educational session on flood district regulations ('Flood District 101') before Eau Claire River LLC returns with a Certified Survey Map to subdivide the nine-acre northern parcel as part of their settlement agreement with the Diocese. Commissioner Dick raised concern that the commission understand fill and flood zone restrictions before approving any future subdivision. Nathan Sandwick also flagged the need to update the village's conditional use permit tracking spreadsheet, which had not been maintained in several years.

title: Economic Development Meeting
overview: The Wausau Economic Development Committee met on November 4th and took action on three substantive items: authorizing staff to prepare a TID 8 project plan amendment for infrastructure projects, approving the $1 purchase of a tax-delinquent property at 108 Myron Street for future affordable housing, and debating a deed restriction and resolution for city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue. The Cleveland Avenue item resulted in a procedural deadlock, with a 2-2 tie on the amended resolution, sending the matter to the full city council on November 24th with section 4 removed from the deed restriction.

discussions.item: Approval of October 6th Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: A motion to approve was made by Alder Neil and seconded by Alder Killian (noted in transcript as 'Kellian'). No discussion occurred and the minutes were approved by voice vote.

discussions.item: TID 8 Project Plan Amendment
discussions.body: Director Fifick explained the amendment would authorize staff to engage a consultant to draft a project plan amendment for Tax Increment District 8, adding infrastructure project costs including lead service line replacement, asphalt overlay, 17th Avenue reconstruction, water and sewer upgrades, and traffic signal replacement. Alder Killian expressed she was not prepared to vote without knowing whether lead line replacement funding covered private or entire replacement, but the motion carried 3-1. Staff noted the item had already been approved 5-0 at the Finance Committee and was placed on the November city council agenda.

discussions.item: Purchase of County-Owned Property at 108 Myron Street
discussions.body: Staff member Tammy presented details on the tax-delinquent property, which has been vacant for years due to a broken pipe causing black mold, rendering it too dangerous to enter. The county approved the city's $1 offer unanimously on October 20th, with full county board consideration set for November 10th. Funding for purchase and demolition would come from Community Development Block Grant funds, not tax levy, with DPW performing the demolition. The end goal is disposition for affordable housing for income-qualifying households. Alder Killian expressed safety concerns about demolition given the black mold but said she would support the motion. Alder Lukans noted for viewers that CDBG/HUD funds, not taxpayer levy money, would be used. The motion carried unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Deed Restriction and Resolution for 1300 Cleveland Avenue
discussions.body: Director Fifick and the committee debated a draft deed restriction prohibiting industrial uses on the city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue, while preserving existing non-conforming uses including Marathon County/Wausau Parks log and wood chip storage and DPW training approved by a 2024 resolution. Alder Tierney's written comments, read into the record by Director Fifick, argued that non-conforming uses should end and the property cleaned up as promised to neighbors. Parks representative Jamie testified that relocating log storage requires council direction on an alternative site of approximately one acre, noting the ongoing Emerald Ash Borer program creates continuous need. Mayor Diny reported that fire training had already been relocated, and miscellaneous DPW equipment and a trailer had been cleaned up. Alder Killian moved an amendment to remove section 4A from the deed restriction, discontinue DPW training by February 1st, and give Parks 6 months to relocate; that amendment failed 2-2. Chair Heniki then moved a narrower amendment to remove only section 4 from the deed restriction, which passed 3-1. The main motion on the resolution as amended then failed 2-2, sending the matter to the November 24th city council meeting with section 4 removed from the deed restriction and a redrafted resolution to be prepared by staff.
